title: The `case` Statement 🗂️
description: Branch elegantly with pattern matching. Perfect for menus and command parsing.

slides.title: When `if` Gets Too Long 🧵
slides.content:
## Enter `case`

Imagine testing a variable against many fixed values. An `if-elif` ladder can become ugly. `case` is a cleaner alternative.

It compares a value against patterns and executes the matching block.

Think of it as a more powerful switch statement from other languages.

slides.title: case Syntax
slides.content:
```bash
case $variable in
  pattern1)
    commands;;
  pattern2)
    commands;;
  *)
    default commands;;
esac
```
`;;` ends each block. `esac` (case backwards) closes.

quizData.question: What terminates a pattern block inside a `case`?
quizData.explanation: Each pattern's commands end with a double semicolon `;;`.

slides.title: Powerful Pattern Matching 🎯
slides.content:
## Beyond Fixed Strings

`case` supports shell patterns (globs):
- `*` – matches any string.
- `?` – matches any single character.
- `[abc]` – character class.
- `[a-z]` – range.
- `|` – separates multiple patterns (or).

Use `*` as the catch‑all default.

slides.title: File Type Checker

quizData.question: In `case`, which symbol separates multiple patterns that should trigger the same action?
quizData.explanation: The pipe `|` acts as an OR between patterns, e.g., `jpg|png)` matches either.

slides.title: A Complete Menu Script 📋
slides.content:
## Practical Use‑Case

`case` shines when building simple text menus. You can present options and let the user choose.

slides.title: Menu Demo
Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `;;&` (Bash 4.0+) to fall through and test the next pattern, or `;&` to execute the next block unconditionally.
